The question is about a pair of sequences that satisfy

$$ A_k = A_{k-1}B_{k-2}+A_{k-2}B_{k-1}, \\ B_k = A_{k-1}B_{k-2}-A_{k-2}B_{k-1} \tag1 $$

for $k=2,3,\dots.$ Now assume that the initial values $A_0,A_1,B_0,B_1$ are arbitrary. Using the equations in $(1)$ for $k=2,3,4$ produces the factorization

$$ A_4 = 2A_1B_1(A_0B_1(A_0+B_0)-A_1B_0(A_0-B_0)). \tag2 $$

But $A_0,A_1,B_0,B_1$ were arbitrary; implying, by the same argument, that $A_{k+3}$ is always divisible by $A_kB_k$ if $k>0$. The rest follows the same as in the answer by Terry Tao.

Also, the Will Jagy answer notes that equation $(2)$ can be simplified to

$$ A_4 = 2A_1B_1(A_2B_0 - A_0B_2). \tag3 $$

It is indeed true (as observed numerically by Will Jagy) that $A_n$ divides $A_{n+3}$ for all $n \geq 1$, which implies in particular that the $k^\text{th}$ smallest prime factor of $A_n$ is bounded uniformly in $n$. This, combined with the eventual periodicity of $A_n$ mod $p$ for each prime $p$, gives the eventual periodicity of the smallest prime factors (as one only needs to test a bounded number of such primes to determine the $k^\text{th}$ smallest prime factor).

To see this claimed divisibility, work modulo $A_n$. With respect to this modulus, we have \begin{align*} A_{n+1} &= A_n B_{n-1} + A_{n-1} B_n = A_{n-1} B_n\\ B_{n+1} &= A_n B_{n-1} - A_{n-1} B_n = -A_{n-1} B_n\\ A_{n+2} &= A_{n+1} B_n + A_n B_{n+1} = A_{n-1} B_n^2 \\ B_{n+2} &= A_{n+1} B_n - A_n B_{n+1} = A_{n-1} B_n^2 \\ A_{n+3} &= A_{n+2} B_{n+1} + A_{n+1} B_{n+2} = A_{n-1}^2 B_n^3 - A_{n-1}^2 B_n^3 = 0 \end{align*} and so $A_{n+3}$ is divisible by $A_n$ as claimed.
